meta.title: Who really said "Facts are the enemy of truth"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cervantes and not in Don Quixote. It was written by Dale Wasserman for Man of La Mancha (1965) — spoken by his Cervantes-Quixote to Dr Carrasco, and quoted by Wasserman in his own preface. That matters: it is still in copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Facts are the enemy of truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Dale Wasserman wrote it for the 1965 musical Man of La Mancha. There is no Spanish original, because Cervantes never wrote it — and unlike Don Quixote, this line is not free to reuse.

answer.label: Dale Wasserman — Man of La Mancha, 1965
answer.sourceLine: It is not in Don Quixote — not in Cervantes’s Spanish, and not in any English translation, because there is nothing there to translate. The line was written by Dale Wasserman for the musical Man of La Mancha (1965), where his Cervantes-Quixote throws it at Dr Carrasco, who has just said ‘These are facts.’ Wasserman quoted it back in his own preface to the published play. The practical consequence: this sentence is in copyright, while Don Quixote is not.

source.excerpt: Facts are the enemy of truth.
trail: We looked for a Spanish original first, because that is what would settle it. There is none. The phrase has no counterpart in El ingenioso hidalgo Don Quijote de la Mancha (1605 and 1615), and it appears in none of the standard English translations — not Shelton, not Ormsby, not Grossman. A line that exists only in English is a line that was written in English.

It exists in a specific English scene. In Man of La Mancha, Dr Carrasco lays out the case for reality — there are no giants, no kings under enchantment, no chivalry, no knights, and there have been none for three hundred years — and closes with ‘These are facts.’ The reply is the quotation about the musical ↗.

Wasserman then quoted himself. In the preface to the published play he writes that ‘Facts are the enemy of truth,’ says Cervantes-Don Quixote — and that this is precisely what he felt and meant. That hyphenated ‘Cervantes-Don Quixote’ is almost certainly how the misattribution started: a reader takes the name for a citation rather than for the name of a character in a play the published play ↗.
source.excerptNote: Wasserman's line, in the language it was written in. It works on stage because it is an answer to something — Carrasco has just finished a list of facts — and it loses its footing the moment it is lifted out and handed to a seventeenth-century Spaniard as a philosophy.

source.rightsNote: This one genuinely matters. Don Quixote is public domain and so are the older English translations, so people reasonably assume anything Quixote says is free — but this sentence is not from the novel. It is a 1965 American dramatic work by an author who died in 2008, and it remains under copyright for decades yet. Short attributed quotation for comment or review is ordinary practice; putting it on merchandise, in an advertisement, or reproducing dialogue at length is a licensing question, and Man of La Mancha is actively licensed for performance. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Dale Wasserman
author.heading: About Dale Wasserman
author.bio: Dale Wasserman was a self-educated American dramatist — he left school early and rode freight trains before finding his way into theatre — who wrote two enduringly popular stage adaptations: One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest and Man of La Mancha. He was firm that Man of La Mancha was never an adaptation of Cervantes’s novel; it dramatises Cervantes himself, imprisoned and defending his story. Which makes the misattribution a small joke at his expense: his best-known sentence is one almost nobody knows he wrote.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case with an expensive twist: the wrong author is four hundred years old and free to quote, and the right one is modern and is not.

items.why: The sentence does not appear in Don Quixote in Spanish or in any English translation of it. There is no chapter number to give because there is no passage. Quote-aggregator sites list it under Cervantes with no citation at all search the text ↗.

It is dialogue from Man of La Mancha, spoken to Dr Carrasco after his catalogue of facts, and Wasserman quotes it in his preface to the published play. He never claimed Cervantes wrote it — he attributed it to his own character, ‘Cervantes-Don Quixote.’

items.who: A character's name read as a citation
items.why: When a playwright writes a historical figure as a character, everything that character says acquires the historical figure’s authority on the way out of the theatre. The same thing happens to Shakespeare’s Caesar and Bolt’s Thomas More. It is the single commonest route from stage dialogue to fake quotation.

items.who: Public domain is the wrong assumption
items.why: Because the line is credited to a seventeenth-century author, people treat it as free stock text and print it on things. It is a 1965 work whose author died in 2008. The misattribution does not just get the credit wrong — it gets the licensing wrong.

misattribution.truthLine: Written by Dale Wasserman for Man of La Mancha in 1965, not by Cervantes. There is no Spanish original because there was never anything to translate — and the line is still in copyright the source ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a defence of the imagination that arrives dressed as a paradox, and it lands hardest in an argument you are losing on the evidence. Wasserman gives it to a man who has been told, correctly, that giants do not exist — and it is meant to be both magnificent and slightly mad, which is the whole tension of the play.

Detached from Carrasco and pinned on Cervantes, it stops being a character’s defiance and becomes an aphorism, which is a much less interesting thing and a much more useful one to anyone wanting to wave away inconvenient information. Wasserman’s Quixote is not licensing that. He is a knight refusing to stop being a knight.
context.detailsSummary: How a musical line became a Cervantes quotation
detailsBody: 1959: Wasserman writes I, Don Quixote, a non-musical television play about Cervantes in prison.
1965: it becomes Man of La Mancha, with Mitch Leigh’s music and Joe Darion’s lyrics, and runs for years.
In the script, Dr Carrasco itemises reality and ends ‘These are facts.’ The answer is the quotation.
Wasserman’s preface repeats it and calls the speaker ‘Cervantes-Don Quixote’ — his own name for his own character.
Quotation sites drop the hyphen, keep the Cervantes, and the line joins the public domain by mistake.
It has not. Wasserman died in 2008 and the play is still licensed for performance.
context.pull: Cervantes never wrote it. A playwright did, in 1965 — and it is still in copyright.
